stories.headline: Tech stocks slide again as Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's IPO loom
stories.summary: A selloff in technology shares carried into a new week, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures lower Monday morning after fresh losses in Asian artificial-intelligence stocks. Investors are waiting for Nvidia's quarterly results on Tuesday, its first since chief executive Jensen Huang stepped down, and for the pricing of Anthropic's initial public offering, which Bloomberg says is expected Wednesday with trading to start Thursday.
stories.why_it_matters: AI-linked companies make up a large share of the stock indexes that most retirement accounts and index funds track, so a prolonged drop in them shows up in ordinary savers' balances. This week's two events are being treated as a test of whether investors still want to pay high prices for AI growth.
stories.background: Much of the stock market's rise in recent years has come from a handful of companies tied to artificial intelligence, with chipmaker Nvidia the largest of them. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply amid allegations that its chips were diverted to China and the resignation of its longtime chief executive, Jensen Huang. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what outlets describe as a very large offering. Separately, U.S. Treasury yields rose last week after inflation data and comments from Federal Reserve officials led traders to consider the possibility of interest-rate increases. The Nasdaq Composite ended Friday down about 6% over the past month, while the S&P 500 was down about 2%.

facts.text: S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures fell Monday morning ahead of Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's market debut.
The decline followed new weakness in Asian AI-related stocks, and Bloomberg reported that emerging-market stocks had their largest drop in more than a week.
Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, Nov. 17; the company said in a securities filing that the date was unchanged after its chief executive's departure.
Anthropic's IPO is expected to price on Wednesday and begin trading on Thursday, according to Bloomberg.
U.S. Treasury yields fell Monday after rising significantly last week on inflation data and Federal Reserve officials' comments, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The dollar index (DXY) rose to 103.533, which the Wall Street Journal described as a 19-month high.
Gold edged up but stayed near one-year lows after losing 4.5% last week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Economist Jason Furman, a former White House adviser, said that if AI turns out to be a bubble that bursts, the most likely result is a 25% drop in the broader market, MarketWatch reported.
Morgan Stanley strategists, in their outlook for the year ahead, recommended raising stock holdings to the highest possible allocation, MarketWatch reported.

framing.note: Calls Nvidia's results and Anthropic's debut 'tests' and stresses that traders are avoiding risk.
Describes the week as 'crucial' for AI and, in its subheading, points to a leadership crisis at Nvidia.
Takes the opposite angle, leading with a strategist's case that Nvidia remains attractive over the long term.
A neutral live-updates label that does not name a cause for the moves.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent urges Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for a successor to Jensen Huang, who has resigned as chief executive, and called for a "dramatic shakeup" of its leadership. Nvidia has named its finance chief, Colette Kress, interim CEO. The company reports earnings Tuesday and, according to the New York Post, has 10 days to answer the administration's questions about banned chip sales.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world and a large holding in most index funds, so who runs it and how its dispute with the government ends affects many people's savings. It is unusual for a Treasury secretary to say publicly how a private company should choose its chief executive.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most artificial-intelligence systems, and U.S. rules limit which of them can be sold to China. The company has faced allegations that restricted chips reached China through a Singapore-based buyer called Megaspeed; Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for more than three decades, has now stepped down amid the controversy. The Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, enforces the export rules, and Bessent has criticized that department's handling of the matter. Nvidia's board must now choose a permanent chief executive.

facts.text: Bessent said Nvidia must "go outside the company" to find its next chief executive.
He called for a "dramatic shakeup" at the company.
Bessent has criticized the Commerce Department under Howard Lutnick over suspected diversion of chips to China while defending President Trump's handling of the matter, CNBC reported.

Nvidia said in a securities filing that Huang had stepped down, that chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and that director Harvey Jones became the company's first board chair.
The New York Post reported that Nvidia must answer the administration within 10 days on whether it profited from banned chip sales.
The Washington Post reported that President Trump's holdings of Nvidia stock grew to as much as $62 million before the scandal became public.

framing.note: Sticks to Bessent's own words about going outside the company.
Leads with the 'dramatic shakeup' phrase; its summary highlights the rift between Bessent and the Commerce Department.
Labels the affair a 'China chip scandal' in the headline.
Turns attention to the president's personal financial stake in the company.

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: wire report of Bessent's call for an outside CEO.
Headline and summary only: adds Bessent's criticism of Lutnick's department and defense of Trump.
Headline and summary only: notes Huang's resignation and a 10-day deadline for Nvidia to respond to the administration.
Headline only: frames Bessent's remarks as a call for a leadership shake-up amid a China chip scandal.
Headline only (paywalled): its own reporting on the size of Trump's Nvidia holdings.

stories.headline: Japan's economy shrinks unexpectedly as energy costs squeeze households
stories.summary: Japan's economy contracted at an annualized rate of 0.1% in the July-September quarter, a preliminary government estimate showed Monday. Outlets described the decline as unexpected and attributed it to weak consumer spending as high energy prices and inflation cut into household budgets. The Financial Times said the result complicates the Bank of Japan's plans for interest rates.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is one of the world's largest economies and a major U.S. trading partner, and its central bank's decisions affect global bond markets and the value of the dollar against the yen. The figures also show how higher oil prices linked to the Iran war are weighing on consumers outside the United States.
stories.background: Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures the total value of goods and services an economy produces; the annualized rate shows what a quarter's change would amount to over a full year. Japan imports nearly all of its oil and gas, so it is exposed when energy prices rise, as they have since the war involving Iran disrupted supplies. The Bank of Japan, led by Governor Kazuo Ueda, has been weighing interest-rate increases to contain inflation, but a shrinking economy makes that harder to justify. The figure released Monday is a first estimate and will be revised.

facts.text: Japan's economy contracted at an annualized rate of 0.1% in July-September, according to the preliminary estimate.
Reuters and CNBC described the contraction as unexpected.
It was the first quarterly contraction in a year, the Financial Times reported.
Outlets linked the decline to pressure on households from inflation and high energy and oil prices.
CNBC reported that household energy subsidies had expired in September, leaving consumers more exposed to higher prices.
The Financial Times also cited record-breaking rains as a drag on growth and said the data complicates interest-rate plans.
Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda told a government panel that wage growth was "quite strong," Reuters reported.
The Cabinet Office's release calendar lists a second, revised estimate for Dec. 8.

framing.note: Stresses that the result was a surprise and puts inflation's effect on households first.
Says the economy contracted only 'slightly' and points to high oil prices.
Emphasizes that it is the first contraction in a year; the summary adds weather and weak spending as causes.
Puts elevated energy costs in the headline as the cause.

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: wire flash with the 0.1% annualized figure.

stories.headline: Diesel falls below $6 a gallon for the first time since early September
stories.summary: The average U.S. retail price of diesel dropped below $6 a gallon, its lowest level in about two months. The New York Post attributed the decline to easing tensions and weaker demand. Separately, Goldman Sachs forecast that oil prices will fall next year as supply outpaces demand.
stories.why_it_matters: Diesel powers the trucks, trains and farm equipment that move and produce most goods, so its price feeds into what people pay for food and deliveries. Bloomberg described it as a key source of the inflation that has raised energy and food prices this fall.
stories.background: Diesel prices climbed sharply this year after the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran disrupted oil supplies and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries reduced fuel production, according to the New York Post. Because diesel is used throughout the supply chain, higher prices tend to spread to other goods. U.S. consumer prices were up 3.7% from a year earlier in September, and Treasury yields rose last week on concerns that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates. Crude oil has already come down from its highs, with Brent crude near $92 a barrel in the latest data.

facts.text: U.S. retail diesel fell below $6 a gallon, the lowest in about two months and the first time under that level since early September.
The New York Post attributed the drop to easing tensions and weaker demand.
Bloomberg called diesel a key inflationary input that has pushed energy and food prices higher this fall.
Goldman Sachs said the oil market faces a "sizable surplus" in 2027 and forecast Brent crude averaging $88 a barrel next year, easing to $78 by year-end, Bloomberg reported.

framing.note: Headline gives the reasons for the drop: easing tensions and weaker demand.
Headline emphasizes the consequence, relief on inflation, more than the cause.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: reports the two-month low and recalls why diesel surged.
Headline and summary only (paywalled): presents the decline as easing a key inflation pressure.
Headline and summary only (paywalled video): Goldman Sachs's forecast of an oil surplus and lower Brent prices.

stories.headline: Intel shareholders sue after 29% share drop tied to slowing PC sales
stories.summary: Shareholders have sued Intel after its stock fell 29%, Reuters reported. The proposed class action claims the chipmaker hid from investors how much slowing personal-computer sales were hurting its business, according to the BBC. The claims have not been tested in court.
stories.why_it_matters: Intel is one of the largest U.S. chipmakers and is widely held in retirement and index funds, so a drop of that size affects many ordinary investors. The suit adds to a difficult stretch for semiconductor stocks more broadly.
stories.background: Intel makes processors for personal computers and data centers and has long depended on PC sales for much of its revenue. When a company's shares fall sharply after bad news, investors often file a class action, a lawsuit brought on behalf of a large group, arguing that executives knew of the problems earlier and did not disclose them. Such cases typically take years, and many are dismissed or settled. The coverage reviewed for this brief does not include Intel's response.

facts.text: Intel was sued by shareholders following a 29% fall in its share price.
The suit is a proposed class action alleging the company concealed the effect of slowing PC sales from shareholders, the BBC reported.

framing.note: Headline centers on the size of the stock drop.
Headline centers on the cause, a slump in PC sales.

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: wire report of the suit and the 29% decline.
Headline and summary only: describes the proposed class action's claim about PC sales.
